summary: Examines how an enterprise can connect to several ISPs over IPv6 with provider-assigned addresses without using network prefix translation. Hosts get an address from each ISP, and source address selection and routing at the site must cooperate. It reviews available mechanisms and their limits.

plainLanguage.summary: If a school has several roads out, each with its own street name, kids must pick the right road for the address on their letter. This explains how.

questions: source address based routing for isps
subtitle: Multihoming with IPv6 provider-assigned addresses without translation.

tldr.problem: Enterprise sites want to connect to multiple ISPs using provider-assigned IPv6 addresses without using Network Prefix Translation (NPT), but ISPs filter source addresses based on who assigned them, and packets with mismatched source addresses are dropped or create asymmetric routing.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts select source addresses based on the destination ISP; routers forward packets by consulting both the source address and destination address (Source Address Dependent Routing, SADR); routers and hosts coordinate using Router Advertisements, DHCPv6, and ICMPv6 to adapt to uplink failures.
tldr.outcome: Enterprise sites can achieve redundant ISP connectivity with provider-assigned addresses, though hosts must actively participate in routing decisions and handle ISP failures differently than with PI addresses or NAT.

facts.label: Hosts per ISP prefix
facts.value: at least one address per host

today: RFC 8678 is an Informational RFC published in December 2019. It remains the primary reference for multihoming with provider-assigned IPv6 addresses without Network Prefix Translation, though SADR routing implementation in production networks is still emerging.

sections.title: Provider-Assigned Multihoming without Translation
sections.content:
Site multihoming is a common enterprise architecture where a site connects to multiple upstream networks for redundancy. With provider-independent (PI) addresses, all traffic uses the same address space regardless of which ISP link it exits through, and multihoming is straightforward. However, provider-independent addresses require more expensive registrations and increase the size of the Internet routing table.

With provider-assigned (PA) addresses, each ISP assigns its own prefix to the site. This is cheaper and preferable from a routing table perspective, but creates problems: (1) ISPs implement BCP 38 ingress filtering, dropping packets with source addresses not assigned by that ISP; (2) if a packet with ISP-A's address exits via ISP-B, the response returns via ISP-A's routing path, breaking two-way communication when ISP-A is down; (3) stateful firewalls break because traffic is asymmetric.

IPv4 typically solves this with NAT or NAPT on the uplinks. This document explores a solution that avoids translation: hosts choose source addresses based on which ISP they want to use, and routers forward based on both source and destination addresses (SADR). This approach requires new routing functionality but eliminates translation overhead and complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ISP gives you a street name (prefix). To use ISP-A, you pick an address in ISP-A's prefix as your source address so packets aren't filtered. The router also looks at the source prefix to decide which ISP road to send packets on.

sections.title: Requirements and Concepts
sections.content:
Source Address Dependent Routing (SADR) is routing that takes the source address into account in addition to the destination address. An SADR domain is a routing domain where some (or all) routers exchange source-dependent routing information. A Source-Prefix-Scoped Routing/Forwarding Table contains information applicable only to packets with source addresses from a specific prefix.

A Site Edge Router (SER) connects the site to an ISP uplink. Provider-assigned (PA) address space comes from an ISP's allocation and is typically provider-aggregatable; it is cheaper than provider-independent addresses but not globally unique across all ISPs. The solution requires: (1) each host to have multiple addresses (at least one per ISP prefix); (2) hosts to select appropriate source addresses through mechanisms like Router Advertisements, DHCPv6, or ICMPv6 feedback; (3) routers to perform SADR, especially site edge routers and any routers downstream of them that interconnect multiple uplinks.
sections.plainLanguage: SADR is routing that looks at both where a packet came from (source address) and where it's going (destination). Site edge routers must support SADR; other routers may or may not. Each host needs addresses from each ISP.

sections.title: Enterprise Topology and Use Cases
sections.content:
A simple multihoming scenario has a site connected to two ISPs. Each ISP assigns a prefix; each host is assigned addresses from both prefixes. Simple case: two site edge routers (SERa and SERb) are directly connected. Routers in the site can forward destination-based routes normally; only SERa and SERb exchange source-scoped routing information, allowing them to forward traffic with source addresses from the wrong prefix to the correct SER.

More complex topologies may have site edge routers not directly connected; in that case, other routers in the site must also support SADR and form a connected SADR domain. Enterprise operators expect multihomed sites to behave like single-homed sites internally: traffic between internal hosts should be unaffected by multihoming, and internal hosts should be reachable via multiple external paths. For external traffic, operator expectations are that packets exit via the ISP whose prefix matches the source address.

Sites may also have additional services: an ISP may offer access to a private service (e.g., CDN or VPN endpoint) only via a specific uplink. In this case, hosts must use the source address for that ISP to reach the service, requiring more sophisticated host-based routing policy or coordination between host, network, and ISPs.
sections.plainLanguage: A site with two ISPs has two edge routers. If they're directly connected, only they need SADR. If they're not, all routers between them need SADR. Internal traffic ignores ISP prefixes; external traffic respects them.

sections.title: Source-Prefix-Scoped Routing and Forwarding
sections.content:
SERs originate source-prefix-scoped routes in addition to normal unscoped destination routes. A scoped route might be: (S=ISP-A-prefix, D=::/0) meaning "packets with source in ISP-A's prefix destined for anything should exit via ISP-A." Each SADR-capable router builds separate forwarding tables for each source prefix.

Building these tables involves: (1) computing next-hops for scoped destination prefixes using only SADR-domain routers; (2) computing next-hops for unscoped prefixes using all routers; (3) augmenting each source-prefix-scoped forwarding table with entries from less specific tables. When forwarding a packet, the router selects the most specific source-prefix-scoped forwarding table matching the packet's source, then looks up the destination address.

This mechanism allows traffic with different source prefixes to take different paths based on the source prefix-assigned ISP, while internal and incoming traffic use normal destination-based paths. Non-SADR routers in the site can still participate; they use only unscoped routes and forward all traffic destination-based. SADR routers redirect mismatched packets to the correct SER, ensuring all traffic eventually exits the correct uplink.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router maintains separate path tables scoped to source prefixes. When forwarding, it picks the right table based on the source prefix, then looks up the destination. Routers that don't support SADR just use the normal table.

sections.title: Host Source Address Selection
sections.content:
Hosts must select appropriate source addresses for outgoing traffic. RFC 6724 defines algorithms for source and destination address selection based on address properties and a policy table. In multihoming scenarios, four rules are most relevant: avoid deprecated addresses, prefer addresses in a prefix advertised by the next-hop, prefer addresses with matching policy labels, and prefer longest matching prefix with the destination.

Operators can influence source address selection using Router Advertisements: assigning different Prefix Information Options (PIOs) per ISP link and using Route Information Options (RIOs) to associate destination prefixes with next-hops. Operators can also distribute address selection policy tables via DHCPv6 (though not all hosts support this). ICMPv6 provides reactive feedback: if a host chooses the wrong source address, the corresponding SER can send an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable (Code 5: source address failed policy) message, prompting the host to try a different source address.

When uplinks fail, hosts must detect the failure and switch to a different source address (and thus a different ISP). Mechanisms include DHCPv6 lifecycle updates, Router Advertisement preferred lifetime deprecation, or ICMPv6 feedback. The challenge is that multihoming without translation requires hosts to react to network failures; hosts cannot simply ignore failures at remote ISP links the way they can with PI-based or NAT-based multihoming.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers advertise which addresses to use; hosts follow those hints or are told via ICMPv6 when they picked wrong. If an ISP link fails, hosts must switch to the other ISP's address or lose connectivity.
